A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same APT study. The main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original APT experiments, including subsurface prediction, architectural ablations, super-resolution, out-of-distribution evaluation and cross-dataset training.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, scaling experiments, computational measurements and standard PDE benchmark results.

M1.justification: The fused global/local encoder, gating, latent approximator, decoder, temporal conditioning and training objective remain unchanged in Section 2 and Appendix B. The new scaling experiments vary model width without introducing a new APT component or procedure.

E1.justification: New Appendix D adds Airfoil, Darcy and Elasticity evaluations, covering compressible flow, linear porous-medium flow and linear solid mechanics. This substantially extends task coverage beyond the retained subsurface and CarBench experiments. The scaling studies reuse ATES.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Transolver, MINO, UPT and HOOD to the faulted CO2 comparison. Table 3 adds evaluated UPT and Transolver baselines on ATES and records an attempted MINO evaluation that exceeds memory capacity. These additions substantially broaden comparisons on existing tasks; the earlier comparators remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.5 introduces controlled experiments with 40k, 120k and 161k training samples and 0.8M, 17.5M and 69.4M parameters, reporting the best test loss during training. New baseline experiments specify additional training budgets and configurations. The faulted-CO2 timing protocol changes its reported GPU from A100 to H100, except HOOD on A100, and newly specifies batch size 340; these are not directly comparable timing conditions across versions.

E4.justification: Section 4.5 and Table 7 add data-size and model-capacity sensitivity studies, testing whether additional data and parameters continue improving ATES predictions. Section 4.3 also expands analysis of accuracy, latency and memory tradeoffs. Existing branch ablations, super-resolution tests, geological distribution-shift tests and qualitative cases are retained.

E5.justification: No changed run counts, seeds, uncertainty estimators, confidence intervals or significance procedures are documented. The existing uncertainty descriptions and CarBench sampling-seed caveat remain. Changes to CarBench uncertainty values are numerical result changes, without evidence of a changed estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline, scaling, efficiency and PDE results while retaining the main APT accuracy scores. Table 7 reports losses falling from 0.1153 to 0.0812 with increased data and from 0.1167 to 0.0722 with increased model size. CarBench changes from 96.00±3.1 to 96.00±0.18 for R2 and from 0.1535±0.038 to 0.1535±0.0022 for relative L2. The timing table replaces APT's 0.017 s with 0.002 s under different hardware. New Table 17 places APT second on Airfoil and Elasticity but third on Darcy, contrary to its caption.

T1.justification: The operator formulation, loss, conditioning equations, metric definitions and governing-PDE assumptions in Section 2 and Appendices B–C are retained. The new mesh-adaptivity taxonomy is descriptive and introduces no new formal result, proof or derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract adds an explicit claim of favorable scaling behavior and narrows the first-architecture claim from adaptive mesh refinement generally to HR-adaptive simulations. The central claims about fused attention, mesh flexibility, super-resolution and cross-dataset learning remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new scaling results as showing further growth potential and explains MINO's ATES memory failure through its mesh-dependent latent size. Appendix D emphasizes that APT's advantage is strongest in heterogeneous subsurface settings. The conclusion newly acknowledges that scaling was demonstrated for one physics type and leaves multiphysics pretraining and transfer fine-tuning untested.

D1.justification: Appendices C.1.2 and C.2.1 substantially expand implementation documentation for the added baselines, including widths, layers, tokens, graph hierarchy, optimizer settings and training budgets. v2 also specifies timing batch size and hardware and documents scaling configurations. Existing APT implementation descriptions and the promise to release code and created datasets upon publication remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds HOOD and MINO citations and introduces Appendix A.5 distinguishing R-, H- and HR-adaptivity. It explicitly credits UPT's earlier ability to query different input/output mesh topologies, refining APT's novelty positioning. Other reference changes largely update bibliographic metadata or remove duplicate entries.

P1.justification: v2 adds focused efficiency and scaling subsections, a mesh-adaptivity subsection, Appendix D and a limitations paragraph. Existing prose and section organization are largely retained, with localized grammar, reference and conference-header edits.

P2.justification: v2 adds the accuracy–latency–memory plot in Figure 4 and new scaling and PDE tables, while expanding the baseline and timing tables with rows, groups and footnotes. Existing figures and most table designs are retained, with localized relocation, renumbering and page reflow.

improvement.justification: The added mesh-native comparisons in Tables 1 and 3 address an important weakness in v1's evidence for its central subsurface claims: limited comparison with closely related operators. Scaling experiments, broader PDE evaluations and explicit applicability limits further strengthen the paper. These substantial gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including best-test-loss selection in the scaling study, Table 17's incorrect ranking caption, and unexplained CarBench uncertainty changes that conflict with the retained discussion of unusually large deviations.
